entries.claim: Plausible Analytics is built to enable customers to comply with GDPR, CCPA and other privacy regulations that impact their business.
entries.verbatim: Plausible Analytics is a privacy-first web analytics startup that’s built to enable you to comply with GDPR, CCPA and other privacy regulations that impact your business.

entries.claim: Plausible encrypts data in transit using TLS 1.2 or newer, with TLS 1.3 preferred.
entries.verbatim: In transit we use TLS 1.2 or newer, with TLS 1.3 preferred.

entries.claim: Plausible uses hashing techniques so visitor data cannot be reversed or used to identify individuals, with rotating salts adding extra protection.
entries.verbatim: We use hashing techniques to ensure that visitor data cannot be reversed or used to identify individuals. The use of rotating salts adds an additional layer of protection.

entries.claim: Plausible generates a daily changing identifier from the visitor's IP address and User-Agent, anonymized by running them through a hash function with a rotating salt.
entries.verbatim: We generate a daily changing identifier utilizing the visitor’s IP address and User-Agent. To anonymize these data points and make them impossible to relate to the user, we run them through a hash function with a rotating salt.

entries.claim: Plausible rotates and deletes the hashing salt every 24 hours.
entries.verbatim: The salt is rotated and deleted every 24 hours.

entries.claim: Plausible never stores the raw IP address and User-Agent in logs, databases or anywhere on disk.
entries.verbatim: The raw IP address and User-Agent are never stored in logs, databases or anywhere on disk.

entries.claim: All visitor data is kept encrypted in Germany on servers owned by Hetzner, a German company.
entries.verbatim: All visitor data is kept encrypted in Germany on servers owned by a German company (Hetzner).

entries.verbatim: You retain full ownership and control of your website data.

entries.verbatim: You can export aggregated stats at any time in [CSV format](https://plausible.io/docs/export-stats) or query them using our [stats API](https://plausible.io/docs/stats-api).

entries.claim: Enterprise customers can receive individual event records through scheduled raw event data exports delivered daily to their S3-compatible storage.
entries.verbatim: Enterprise customers who need individual event records can use [scheduled raw event data exports](https://plausible.io/docs/raw-data-export), delivered daily to their S3-compatible storage.

segments.name: A freelance SEO/web consultant who dreads opening GA4 in front of a client
segments.situation: They look after analytics for a roster of client sites they mostly didn't build. The reporting tool is GA4, and the consultant is the one who has to make it legible: explorations to configure, a UI the client cannot navigate alone, and data that isn't there when the client asks about this morning's campaign. One consultant in this position describes Plausible as his "100% favorite GA4 alternative so far", specifically because it is "SOOOO easy to use (for clients too)" and "the data is near real-time", and calls it a fit for "~70% of websites struggling with GA4" — so the struggle he is describing is the client's, not only his own. The same person concedes in the same breath that the alternative is "not free and not a ton of bells and whistles", which is the trade he is consciously making. Beyond that quote, the shape of their week — how many clients, how long reporting takes, what they bill for it — is not documented here and should not be invented.

objections.objection: "Google Analytics is free. I'd be paying monthly, forever, for a tool with fewer features."
objections.answer: Partly answerable, and the gap should not be hidden. On price: entry pricing is published ($9/month Starter, $14 Growth, $19 Business at the 10k-pageview tier), yearly billing saves two months, there are no long-term contracts, and plan and tier changes in either direction are pro-rated so a wrong guess is not punished [E328, E329, E330, E275, E270, E296, E297, E299]. On risk of trying: the 30-day trial has no card on file, cannot auto-convert and has nothing to cancel [E45, E47, E48, E49]. On "fewer features": a consultant who bought it says exactly that — "not free and not a ton of bells and whistles" — and bought anyway because the tool was usable by his clients and the data was near real-time [E318]. Nothing in the evidence justifies the price in money terms: there is no cost-of-time study, no ROI case study, no customer saying what the switch was worth financially. The honest argument is usability and privacy, not savings.

objections.objection: "It can't answer the questions my boss or client asks. No user-level data, no real attribution depth — I'd move and then need GA back anyway."
objections.answer: Answerable up to a line, and the line matters. Available: funnels with drop-off across a fixed sequence, user journeys, ecommerce revenue tracking attributed to traffic sources, custom properties, saved filters and segments, scroll depth, UTM campaigns with automatic channel grouping, Search Console queries in the dashboard, period comparison, AI-assistant traffic as a channel [E221, E222, E214, E219, E260, E303, E306, E305, E237, E259]. Where it stops: funnels, user journeys, revenue tracking, custom properties and the Stats API require the Business plan [E273, E330]; event- and session-level raw data is Enterprise-only, delivered daily to the customer's own S3 storage, and cannot be bought as an add-on [E10, E281, E277]. A paying consultant publicly agrees it is "not a ton of bells and whistles" [E318] — do not argue with that, scope it.

objections.objection: "I'm not throwing away years of history. If I switch, my year-on-year comparisons break."
objections.answer: Directly answered: Google Analytics history can be imported so the new dashboard starts with the full data record, stats can also be imported via CSV, and periods can be compared against previous ranges once the history is in [E199, E225, E321, E226, E237]. What the evidence does not say is which GA metrics survive the import, at what granularity, or whether imported and native data are comparable — so do not promise fidelity.

objections.objection: "Switching is an afternoon I don't have: a new snippet on every site, every goal rebuilt, GTM touched, dashboards re-shared."
objections.answer: Answered for the install, partly for the rest. One lightweight snippet in the header covers a domain and its subdomains; there is an official WordPress plugin (excludes your own visits, stats inside the WP dashboard, no conflict with WP Rocket), an official GTM template requiring no code change, an official NPM tracker for React/Vue/Next.js, guides for Shopify, Webflow, Squarespace, Wix, Ghost, Hugo and more, and a testing tool to verify the install [E189, E98, E191, E192, E193, E99, E102, E195, E206, E198]. Goals: any page can become a goal and file downloads, form completions and outbound link clicks are tracked automatically without extra setup [E308, E217, E215, E216]. Team access is an invite rather than a shared login, and client access can be a shared link [E200, E15]. No evidence quantifies migration time for anyone — the fastest documented decision is one founder paying "within 1hr of the 30-day trial" [E319], which is his experience, not a benchmark.

objections.objection: "A team of ten with no investors. If they fold or get bought, my analytics go with them."
objections.answer: This is the best-evidenced answer available. The code is open source under AGPLv3, publicly inspectable, and the company frames that as the reason you are never locked in and can fork if it ever goes against its stated values [E251, E252, E32, E327]. Commercially: self-funded and profitable, no outside investors, no acquisition targets, subscription revenue is the only revenue, running since 2018, crossed $1M ARR in 2022 [E248, E326, E249, E246]. Scale: 21,000 paying subscribers, 313 billion pageviews tracked, 99.99% uptime over the last 90 days, with Stripe, Mozilla, MongoDB, Harvard and Sentry named among users [E312, E313, E314, E311, E241]. Exit is practical, not theoretical: aggregated stats export to CSV or via the Stats API at any time [E9, E227]. Caveats to respect — "no plans to sell" is an intention, not a commitment, the headcount figure is undated, the subscriber and revenue figures are self-reported, and the customer-name list carries no detail on scope of use [E248, E247, E240, E246, E241].

objections.objection: "Our security review needs SOC 2 or ISO 27001 and an uptime SLA. A security page isn't evidence."
objections.answer: Not answerable with what we have, and this should be said plainly downstream. There is no SOC 2, ISO 27001, or any third-party audit or certification anywhere in the evidence; the compliance page only names GDPR, CCPA and data processing as topics, and the GDPR/CCPA line is explicitly a self-description rather than a certification [E213, E1]. There is no SLA either — Plausible states it aims for continuous availability but does not guarantee uninterrupted service [E31]. All that can be offered instead is self-published practice: 99.99% uptime over the last 90 days, TLS 1.2+ in transit, AES-256 encrypted EU backups retained 30 days with quarterly restore tests, breach notification within 48 hours, role-based access with zero-trust internal access, and open source code for independent review [E314, E2, E20, E21, E25, E17, E18, E32]. None of that closes a procurement checklist, and copy should not pretend otherwise.

objections.objection: "We need SSO for a 15-person team and it's locked behind a sales call."
objections.answer: Confirmed rather than resolved: SSO is an Enterprise plan feature, is not available on Starter, Growth or Business, and cannot be purchased as an add-on — if you need it, Enterprise is required and Enterprise pricing is "Custom", via contact [E55, E277, E331, E274]. Enterprise also has no published price, so there is no way for this buyer to self-qualify on cost. What can be offered without Enterprise: enforced two-factor authentication across all team members, named roles and permissions, active-session listing and remote logout [E88, E89, E90, E13, E15, E14]. The nearest honest move is an ask — contact us — not a workaround.

objections.objection: "Billing by pageviews means a good month turns into a surprise bill or a locked dashboard."
objections.answer: Mostly answered, with one real sting to disclose. Tier is based on total pageviews plus custom events across all sites in a team, and pageview goals don't count toward usage [E285, E286, E287]. There is never an extra charge for an occasional spike, no surprise fees and no stats interruption; a single month over the limit needs no action if traffic falls back the next month, and an early notice appears in account settings [E290, E291, E292]. Two consecutive months over means an upgrade request, pro-rated to the remaining cycle [E293]. The sting: if you don't upgrade within a week of that notice, dashboards are temporarily locked — stats keep collecting in the background, settings stay accessible, and dashboards unlock automatically at the next billing cycle if usage falls back [E294, E295]. Say the lock out loud; a reader who discovers it later stops trusting the rest.

objections.objection: "It's open source and AGPL — I'll just self-host it for free."
objections.answer: Largely unanswered by the evidence. Nothing in the ledger compares self-hosting to the hosted plans: there is no feature comparison, no total-cost argument, no statement about what the community edition includes or omits, and no customer saying they tried self-hosting and came back. The only adjacent facts are that the code is AGPLv3 and forkable [E251, E252, E327], and that Plausible runs the hosted service itself — EU hosting on Hetzner servers, infrastructure management and software development not outsourced, daily backups with quarterly restore tests, 24/7 monitoring with on-call paging, DDoS shielding at the CDN edge, updates multiple times per week [E7, E43, E42, E19, E21, E29, E30, E33]. Those describe operational work a self-hoster would inherit, which is an argument the writer must make themselves; it is not evidenced as a buyer's reason to pay.

objections.objection: "Adblockers will eat my numbers and they won't match what I see in Google Analytics, so nobody internally will trust the new dashboard."
objections.answer: Partly answered. The script can be served as a first-party connection from your own domain to bypass adblockers, and Enterprise can have that proxy set up and maintained for you [E103, E196, E280]. Bots, referrer spam and data center traffic are excluded out of the box so the stats reflect human visits [E310]. There is also a server-side events API that avoids JavaScript entirely [E104, E197]. What the evidence does not provide is any figure for how much traffic adblockers hide, or any statement that Plausible and Google Analytics numbers reconcile — expect a discrepancy and do not promise parity.

objections.objection: "Not now — I'll start the trial and deal with it later." (And if I don't decide in 30 days, what happens to the data I collected?)
objections.answer: Answered precisely, which makes it usable as a deadline rather than a threat. The trial is 30 days with full Business features and limits, no card, no auto-conversion and nothing to cancel [E45, E46, E47, E48, E49]. If nobody subscribes, the dashboard locks but login still works; stats collection stops and dashboards and all their stats are eventually deleted permanently, with an email beforehand so there is time to subscribe or export; subscribing before deletion unlocks the dashboards and keeps the history, and deleted stats cannot be recovered [E50, E52, E53]. The account and all site data can also be deleted in a few clicks at any point [E54, E11]. Note the trap for the "later" reader: a trial started and ignored costs them the history they accumulated, and the retention window before deletion is not specified anywhere in the evidence [E51].

objections.objection: "We're a nonprofit / university / open-source project — there's no budget line for analytics at all."
objections.answer: Answered, but narrowly and with conditions worth stating up front: a 15% discount exists only for nonprofits, educational institutions and open-source projects, only on a Business plan with annual billing, only for new subscriptions, and it is applied via a discount code after contacting them with the organisation name, type, website and chosen pageview tier [E264, E265, E266, E276]. Annual billing itself saves two months, so the two stack [E265, E275]. It continues on renewal as long as the plan doesn't change, and ends on any upgrade or downgrade [E267]. Harvard University and the Python Software Foundation are named among users [E241]. Monthly billing and every non-Business plan are excluded — say so rather than letting the reader discover it at checkout [E266].
